title: Can a mother forget? (Isaiah 49:15–16)
hookLine: even if she did, I will not forget you: engraved on my palms

lines: THREE IN THE MORNING, ONE SMALL SOUND.
cards: Three in the morning. A baby stirs in the next room, makes one small sound, and the mother is awake before she knows why. She can sleep through traffic, thunder, a neighbor's party.
Not that sound. The body seems to keep listening even when the mind is off. It's about as close as everyday life gets to a love that can't forget.
Now set beside it a whole people who feel completely forgotten: far from home, their city in ruins, their prayers going nowhere. And they say so, out loud, to God.

teach.h: ZION: THE LORD HATH FORGOTTEN ME.
teach.b: This part of Isaiah speaks to the people exiled in Babylon, and Jerusalem, called Zion, is pictured as a grieving woman. She says, in the King James Bible: "The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me."
It's a raw line, and the Bible lets it stand.
God answers with a question: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee."

Not a king, not a judge: a nursing mother. Some readers point out that the Hebrew word for compassion is related to the word for womb, so the language itself carries a mother's body. Then the passage goes further.

teach.h: THEY MAY FORGET; I WILL NOT.
teach.b: Even a mother's love can fail; the text admits it. God's memory is stronger than that. Then the second picture: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands."
Graven means engraved, cut in, like letters in stone. Not a note on the back of a hand that washes off.

teach.h: A NAME CARVED INTO THE PALM.
teach.b: A name carved into the palm, permanent, in the one place you see every time you reach for something. Jewish readers hear God's promise never to abandon Zion and its people.

teach.h: I HAVE GRAVEN THEE UPON THE PALMS OF MY HANDS.
teach.b: Christians read it that way too, and some also think of the wounds in Jesus's hands, palms that carry the mark of love. Either way, the answer to Zion's complaint isn't an argument.
It's a hand, held up, with her name on it.

how: Some churches read Isaiah 49:15–16 for comfort and on Mother's Day, and Christians point to it when describing God's love with a mother's tenderness.

o: a strict sense of duty to one's family
tender care, a word related to womb
pity felt from a distance for a stranger

games.q: what's inside Isaiah 49 — tap the pairs.

s: the Bible never pictures God like a mother
Isaiah 49 compares God's love to a nursing mother's, and says it's even stronger.
Isaiah admits that human mothers can forget
"yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee."
the name is written on the back of God's hand
it's graven, carved, on the palms.

games.q: you're Zion, far from home, city in ruins, and you've said it out loud: God has forgotten me. how does God answer?
o: with a question about a mother, and hands with your name carved on them.
games.why: "can a woman forget her sucking child?" even if she could, "yet will I not forget thee." and the name is graven on God's palms.

practice: Open your hands in your lap, palms up, and look at the lines, the creases, the marks of whatever work you've done.
Picture there the name of someone you never want to forget, and then, if it fits, your own name carved in a palm you can't see, held by someone who remembers you.
If you pray, rest in the promise, I will not forget thee; if not, notice what it feels like to be held in someone's memory.

wordCard.voice: Compassion. The Hebrew word that shares its root with womb, used for the care God says will not fail, even if a mother's might.

orig.note: Hebrew: compassion. it comes from the same root as the word for womb.

carryVoice: Your line: engraved on his hands. Not a note that washes off. See you tomorrow.
